claims.text: An ab initio solid–liquid coexistence method can calculate the melting properties of refractory materials.
The coexistence method can determine melting temperature.
The coexistence method can determine entropy and enthalpy of fusion.
The coexistence method can determine the volume change at melting.
The coexistence method is more computationally efficient than full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The material initially has a crystalline solid phase near ambient conditions.
A simulation cell can be initialized with coexisting solid and liquid regions and brought toward the melting point by changing temperature or cell conditions.
The coexistence calculation can be performed with ab initio molecular dynamics in constant-energy or constant-pressure ensembles.
Coexisting solid and liquid regions form a solid–liquid interface.
The dynamics of the solid–liquid interface control the simulated melting process.
Evolution of the coexisting phases under temperature changes reveals the onset of melting through interface dynamics.
Observed changes in the coexistence simulation permit extraction of thermodynamic melting quantities.
The predicted melting properties will agree with targeted experimental estimates.
Full ab initio free-energy calculations using thermodynamic integration are computationally expensive.
The accuracy or applicability of the coexistence method may be limited by simulation-cell size.
The accuracy or applicability of the method may be limited by how well the DFT description represents the solid–liquid interface under extreme conditions.
The accuracy of coexistence-derived thermodynamic quantities relative to full thermodynamic integration is not fully established, particularly for complex refractory systems.
